newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian Chancellor Vranitzky seen ready to resign.
newsitem.headline: Austrian Chancellor Vranitzky seen ready to resign.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, said to be tired of politics after 10 years in office, was expected to offer his resignation on Saturday, a senior source inside his Social Democratic Party said.
"I would assume that this will happen," the source, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters.
Reports of Vranitzky's impending resignation in two Austrian dailies on Saturday were "not far from the truth", he added.
Vranitzky, 59, had called a meeting of his party's executive committee at 4 p.m. (1500 GMT) on Saturday, instead of on Sunday evening as originally planned, the source said.
According to reports in newspapers Der Standard and Kurier, Vranitzky was likely to be succeeded as chancellor and Social Democrat leader by Finance Minister Viktor Klima, 49.
Vranitzky's spokesman Karl Krammer declined to comment on the reports. "There is no comment whatsoever from our side. I haven't even spoken to the chancellor myself," he said.
Vranitzky, a former banker and one-time professional basketball player who became chancellor in 1986, has many times been reported to be tired of Austrian politics.
He took over the Austrian government in 1986 from then Chancellor Fred Sinowatz after two years as finance minister.

The youthful-looking Vranitsky was given much of the credit for Austria's economic upswing during his first four years in office and spearheaded a Socialist election victory in 1990 after a campaign focused on his personality.

But after a general election in 1994, support for the Social Democrats nosedived. Analysts blamed the drop in popularity on changes in traditional voting patterns, two budget battles and several resignations in the party.
A frail coalition of Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party collapsed a year later after a bitter row over Austria's growing budget deficit.
Vranitzky led his party to victory in a snap general election in December 1995 but had to renew his alliance with the conservatives.

The uneasy partners last weekend struck a last-minute deal on the sale of the state's controlling stake in flagship bank Creditanstalt to arch-rival Bank Austria, after a lengthy dispute that once again threatened to split the coalition.

The conservatives had opposed the sale to Bank Austria, which is effectively controlled by the Social Democrat-led City of Vienna, but backed down after the Social Democrats offered concessions, including full privatisation of Bank Austria.
Vranitzky was deputy head of Creditanstalt from 1976 to 1981 before a four-year period as chief executive of Laenderbank, which was later merged into Bank Austria.
The sale of Creditanstalt was widely seen as a personal victory for Klima, who became finance minister a year ago.

Since his appointment, Klima has repeatedly been called Vranitzky's "crown prince". But he has insisted he has no plans to succeed Vranitzky, saying he would rather quit politics altogether and return to industry.
